source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1986) Chunking in Soar: the anatomy of a general learning mechanism
finding: Chunking turns the result of subgoal processing into a rule. It was shown to learn search control and operator rules on puzzles and expert-system tasks. The paper adds a macro-operator demonstration on the Eight Puzzle.
numbers: Eight Puzzle macro table learned with 61 chunks when all three transfer types (simple, within-column symmetry, across-column symmetry) work. Across-column symmetry cut chunks from 83 to 61. The full table needed only 3 carefully chosen trials. Allowing non-minimal macros cut it to 54 chunks but lengthened paths by 2 for 14% of problems, by 4 for 26%, by 6 for 7%.
limits: One puzzle domain, hand-picked training trials, no human or LLM comparison. Not a controlled test of whether chunking beats other learners.
agent_relevance: A stored subgoal result can transfer widely, but only if the state is described in separable parts. Coverage costs few items if the encoding is good.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1986) Chunking in Soar (generality section)
finding: Chunk generality depends on how the state is represented and on what the subgoal looked at. If a representation bundles several roles in one slot, learned chunks test irrelevant things and fail to apply where they should. Dead-end search and unneeded preparation also leak irrelevant conditions into the chunk.
numbers: Example: a Korf-style Eight Puzzle vector (tile identity doubles as position index) makes chunks test tile identity, so they miss situations they should cover. No percentages; a qualitative design finding.
quote: failing to apply in situations in which they rightly could
limits: Qualitative analysis, not an experiment. Later Soar versions rebuilt the mechanism (explanation-based behavior summarization).
agent_relevance: When our agent stores a subgoal result, store its trigger as only the facts the result actually used, not the whole context. Searching false paths in a subgoal pollutes the trigger (G2: cite real output).

source: Tambe, Newell, Rosenbloom (1990) The problem of expensive chunks and its solution by restricting expressiveness
finding: Chunking cut the number of steps in all eight tasks but made total run time worse in four of them, because some learned rules were very costly to match. These were the only four such cases found among several dozen Soar tasks.
numbers: Cognitive effect (steps before/after): Eight-puzzle 6.53, 2-Queens 5.21, Grid 13.54, Magic-square 6.59, Syllogisms 11.59, Monkey and bananas 6.20, Water jug 9.13, Farmer 11.09. Computational effect (time per step before/after) was 0.15, 0.06, 0.06, 0.04 in the four bad tasks. Magic-square total speedup 0.25 (four times slower); time per step up by as much as 25 times. Cheap-chunk tasks gained in total time: Syllogisms 10.27, Monkey 5.16, Water jug 5.22, Farmer 5.04 (table layout garbled in extraction; matched by multiplying the two effects).
quote: no guarantees can be given about Soar's performance
limits: One optimised Rete matcher (Soar/PSM-E), 1990. Matching such a rule is NP-hard in the worst case. The pattern is architecture-specific, but the lesson (steps saved can be lost in retrieval cost) is general.
agent_relevance: Learning more reusable subgoals is not free. For an LLM the match cost is context length and retrieval noise. Track total cost (tokens and steps), not only step count.

source: Tambe, Newell, Rosenbloom (1990) The problem of expensive chunks (cause analysis)
finding: Cost came from the match structure of a few rules (large branching, many multi-valued attributes, bad condition order), not from the number of chunks and only weakly from rule size.
numbers: Footprint (rule size) explained only a minor part of the slowdown. Better condition ordering raised the computational effect by a factor of about two to three in the expensive tasks, which stayed expensive.
limits: Analysis uses the k-search model of the Rete match; small task set.
agent_relevance: Cost depends on how a stored item is looked up, not how many items there are. Design the subgoal library index for cheap exact lookup.

source: Tambe, Newell, Rosenbloom (1990) Restricting expressiveness (unique-attribute fix)
finding: Banning multi-valued attributes guaranteed cheap chunks. The price was less general chunks, so more of them were needed. Even so, total run time after learning was much lower.
numbers: Table of nine tasks: run time after chunking fell in the unique-attribute version in the four bad tasks. Chunk counts rose in some tasks (one row appears to show 11 versus 86 chunks; table text is garbled in extraction). Where unique-attribute chunks were less general, extra hand-selected trials were run to reach the same coverage.
limits: Extra trials were hand-chosen to cover missing chunks, which flatters the unique-attribute result. Soar-specific.
agent_relevance: Trade-off: a restricted, easy-to-match trigger format is cheaper and safer but needs more entries. Prefer a simple, strict trigger schema for the subgoal library.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to Soar
finding: Current Soar defines impasse types by what is missing: no operator proposed (state no-change), tie, conflict, and operator no-change. A substate is made, and chunking compiles its result into a rule once the impasse resolves. Chunking requires the substate's decisions to be deterministic, so it is not used when numeric (probabilistic) preferences decided the result.
numbers: Four impasse types. Learned rule types: elaboration, operator proposal, operator evaluation (planning compiled to search control), operator application. The author says analysis overhead is minimal and gains are much greater than costs, citing Assanie (2022); no figures in this document.
quote: chunking requires that substate decisions be deterministic so that they will always create the same result
limits: Review by the architecture's author; the overhead claim is cited, not shown here.
agent_relevance: Two rules for our library: only store a subgoal result when it was produced deterministically (code-checked), and key each entry to an impasse type so the trigger fires at the right state (S6).

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to Soar (explanation-based behavior summarization)
finding: The old chunking was rebuilt as explanation-based behavior summarization so rules are correct relative to the substate reasoning and as general as possible without over-generalizing. Over-general rules were a known risk of the older design.
numbers: No numbers in this document; the rebuild is attributed to Assanie (2022).
limits: Evidence is a pointer to a thesis, not read here.
agent_relevance: Guard against stale or over-broad stored subgoals: record which inputs justified the result and re-check them at reuse (G3).

source: Rosenbloom & Newell (1982) Learning by chunking: summary of a task and a model
finding: A chunking model of a 1023-choice reaction-time task gave power-law practice curves. But the full production-system model was too expensive to run for many trials, so the long curve came from a faster meta-model.
numbers: Seibel human data: 76,725 trials. Meta-model: 13 cycles per trial plus 31 cycles per pattern used; simulated 72,633 trials; a chunk learned with probability 0.01 per opportunity (without this, the task would be learned perfectly in 3 to 4 passes of 1023 trials).
quote: the practice curves are power law in form
limits: The power-law shape rests on a hand-set learning probability and a cost model estimated from a nine-trial run. A model demonstration, not a fit to human data.
agent_relevance: Weak support for any claim that chunk-based speedup follows human practice curves. Do not borrow a learning-rate law from it.

source: Newell & Rosenbloom (1981) Mechanisms of skill acquisition and the law of practice
finding: Claimed the power law of practice fits human skill data in every case compared, and proposed chunking as the common mechanism. Known here only through secondary summaries in search results.
numbers: Not opened. A search summary says power functions beat exponentials in every comparison in their sample.
limits: Not read in this session; full text not found.
agent_relevance: Background only. Verify before citing numbers.

source: Heathcote, Brown, Mewhort (2000) The power law repealed
finding: Rival account: the power law is an artefact of averaging across learners. Fit to individual curves, an exponential fits better. This weakens the data that chunking theory set out to explain.
numbers: From a search summary only: 40 data sets, 7,910 learning series, 475 subjects, 24 experiments; exponential beat power in all unaveraged sets. Not opened.
limits: Could not open the paper (paywall and redirect). Numbers need checking.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a power-law shape for gains from stored subgoals. Measure the curve directly.

source: Evans, Brown, Mewhort, Heathcote (2018) Refining the law of practice
finding: A Bayesian re-analysis reportedly supported a delayed exponential law in a clear majority of paradigms, not a pure power law (search summary).
numbers: Not opened; no figures.
limits: Could not open; secondary summary only.
agent_relevance: Same as above: assume no functional form for subgoal-reuse gains.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2022) Integrating diverse knowledge sources for online one-shot learning of novel tasks
finding: A Soar agent combined human instruction, search and GPT-3. Search results were chunked into control knowledge so the same task needed no search or prompting on repeat. The LLM alone was not reliable enough.
numbers: Every condition except Search+LLM learned all subtasks in one shot; Search+LLM completed 54% of subtasks. GPT-3 goal proposals were accepted 30 to 40% of the time (30% in the depth-4 search condition); action proposals were 96% correct on the first try. Instructor words fell by about 50% in all LLM conditions. Inst+Search(d4)+LLM used 70 instructions versus 76 baseline, 43 of them yes/no, so about half as many goal or action instructions. Total GPT-3 cost under 10 USD.
quote: even with unexceptional acceptance rates for goal responses from the LLM
limits: Simulated tidy-kitchen robot, one task family, GPT-3 text-davinci-002, objects handled independently. No test of stale-chunk effects.
agent_relevance: Closest published use of the impasse-to-chunk loop with an LLM filling the impasse. A yes/no check by a human or code is what made LLM output safe to store (G2, G3).

source: Kirk et al. (2022) failure cases in the Search+LLM condition
finding: When LLM proposals were used without human review, the stored knowledge included wrong goals. Failures were missing context (close a bin that has no lid) and missing state facts (put empty bottles and cans in the fridge).
numbers: Of 16 objects not tidied when the first response was used, 3 were due to the close-bin-without-lid goal and 3 to empty bottles and cans in the fridge. Only 54% of subtasks completed in Search+LLM.
limits: Small sample, one domain.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and G3: do not store a subgoal result the model produced unless code or an outside check passes it.

source: Augmenting cognitive architectures with large language models (AAAI Spring Symposium 2024)
finding: Proposes using an impasse to query an LLM, learn soft-token embeddings, and store them to prevent the next impasse. It is a design proposal with no experiments.
numbers: No measured results. Discusses Soar and Sigma; says Sigma does not yet support chunking.
limits: Position paper only; evaluation is left to future work in an interactive task learning domain.
agent_relevance: Shows the impasse-then-compile idea is being proposed for LLMs, but gives no evidence for it.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2023) Cognitive architectures for language agents
finding: Frames LLM agents with Soar's structure (memory types, decision loop, impasse to subgoal). Describes Soar writing new productions from experience.
numbers: No experiments; a framework paper with a survey table.
limits: Conceptual mapping, no test of chunking in LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Confirms that the main agent-architecture survey offers no direct LLM test of impasse-driven chunking.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks
finding: Curated procedural skills help LLM agents a lot on average, but the gain varies by model and task. Skills the agent wrote for itself did worse than no skills.
numbers: 87 tasks, 8 domains, 18 model-harness configurations, 9,396 trajectories. Pass rate 33.9% without skills versus 50.5% with curated skills (+16.6 pp; range +4.1 to +25.7 pp). Self-generated skills, three configurations: -8.1 pp (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), -11.3 pp (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5 pp (Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro), while curated skills gave +18.2 to +24.8 pp on the same ones.
limits: Self-generated condition tested on only three configurations. The skills were authored in a separate step before the task, not from impasses during a task. 13 of 87 tasks got worse with skills.
agent_relevance: Strongest warning for the subgoal library: model-written stored procedures can hurt. Admit an item only when an outside check supports it (G3, G5).

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: why self-generated skills fail
finding: A trajectory audit blamed self-generated packs that the solver never found, authoring effort that displaced solving, and confidently wrong pack content when used.
numbers: Qualitative audit (Appendix D.6.1) of the three self-generated runs.
limits: Audit method and sample described in the appendix; not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Design for retrieval: stored subgoals must be surfaced at the right moment by a program, not left for the model to look up.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: moderators (quantity, length, domain, base ability)
finding: Fewer, shorter skills worked better. Domain mattered: gains were big where pretraining coverage is thin.
numbers: Skills per task: 1 skill +18.0 pp, 2 to 3 skills +19.0 pp, 4 or more +10.1 pp. Length: compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7 pp. Domains: natural science +28.8, media +24.1, cybersecurity +18.9, software engineering +11.6, mathematics +9.7 pp. A strong base did not always mean a small gain: one config started at 41.1% and gained only +7.1.
limits: Ablations on the same benchmark; domain numbers differ from the survey that cites an earlier version.
agent_relevance: Keep each stored subgoal short and keep the number retrieved per state at one to three.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: when skills hurt
finding: Skills hurt on 13 of 87 tasks. Cause: a single fixed pipeline with no condition for when it applies, or a skill that displaced a stronger default method.
numbers: Largest drops: -7.4 pp (two tasks) and -5.6 pp (four tasks).
limits: Task-level deltas are small-sample.
agent_relevance: Each stored subgoal needs an applicability test and a fallback; this is the analogue of Soar's condition-matched chunk.

source: Xu & Wu (2026) Skill availability and presentation granularity: a controlled SkillsBench study
finding: A partial replication of SkillsBench on a 30-task subset. Having a skill beat none by a clear margin. How detailed the skill was mattered little, and the effect depended on the model.
numbers: GPT-5.5: no skill 31.3%, curated 67.3% (+36.0 pp, CI +20.7 to +52.0); other conditions +26.7 to +30.7 pp. DeepSeek V4-Flash: no skill 26.0%, curated 50.7% (+24.7 pp). Low versus high abstraction: +0.7 pp (GPT-5.5), -6.7 pp (DeepSeek), both CIs cross zero. One worked example added: +0.7 and +1.3 pp. 1,800 rows, 5 trials per cell, 30 tasks.
limits: 30 tasks, two models, curated skills only; powered to detect differences of 8.3 to 16.0 pp. Does not test self-written skills.
agent_relevance: Availability matters more than format. Do not spend effort on wording of a stored subgoal before retrieval is right.

source: Wang, Panaganti, Zhou (2026) More memory, worse agents: error reproduction and anti-persistence
finding: Stored abstractions (rules, summaries, skills) can pass an error forward and regenerate it later. Keeping raw trajectories and rebuilding guidance on demand did better than keeping stored abstractions.
numbers: Nine benchmark-backbone settings (ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld). Mean success: anti-persistence 59.9%, trajectory memory 53.5%, abstraction memory 49.0%, joint memory 49.3%, Reflexion 52.9%. Best in 7 of 9 settings; above trajectory and abstraction memory in all 9. Lowest LLM-call cost.
limits: Three seeds; own method and own baselines. Not a test of Soar-style chunking itself.
agent_relevance: The most direct counter-evidence to a persistent subgoal library: a chunk is a stored abstraction and can reproduce errors. Prefer storing the case with its checked outcome and re-deriving guidance (G2).

source: Chen et al. (2026) Are self-evolving agents continual learners?
finding: Agents that rewrite prompts or skills from feedback gain on the current stream but forget earlier work. Retrieval-based memory avoids forgetting across distant domains but still pulls in foreign items and collides when similar queries need different workflows.
numbers: Four drifting streams (BIRD, BFCL, ScienceWorld). Retrieval within-group similarity 0.80 to 0.95 versus cross-group 0.57 to 0.63, giving 0% foreign retrievals after a block was filled; before a group's block begins, 100% of retrievals are foreign. Late in the compound stream, 52% and 46% of two groups retrieve a foreign memory. After a workflow-conflict block, one prompt-rewriting method fell on BFCL-Base from 29.8% (119/400) to 11.2% (45/400).
limits: Three methods (ReasoningBank, GEPA, Meta-Harness); not a test of chunking. Streams are synthetic drifts.
agent_relevance: Our library needs a stale-item rule: scope each stored subgoal to its trigger and test for collisions, not just similarity.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent workflow memory
finding: Inducing reusable workflows from past successes and giving them to the agent raised success on web tasks and cut steps. Gains were smaller when train and test tasks differed more.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4): 51.1% relative success gain over the BrowserGym baseline (+12.0 points); 7.6% relative over a method with human-written workflows; about 2.0 fewer steps per example. Mind2Web: 24.6% relative step-success gain. Online AWM beat baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as the train-test gap widened. Rule-based versus LM-based induction differed by 0.1 in success on WebArena.
limits: Many WebArena tasks share templates, so in-template gains are expected; the authors say offline AWM is best only when training data match the test distribution.
agent_relevance: Closest working analogue of a chunk library in LLMs, with gains tied to template overlap. Our tests must separate in-template items from new-structure items.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Agents that keep both extracted insights and retrieved successful trajectories beat agents using only one. Which one matters more depends on the task.
numbers: Insights-only versus retrieve-only success: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38%. ExpeL matches Reflexion after three attempts on HotpotQA (40% vs 39%) and beats it on ALFWorld (59% without retries vs 54%). ALFWorld put task: ReAct 50, insights 61, retrieve 73, ExpeL 83. Random example sampling gave a significant drop; task-similarity retrieval was best.
limits: GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 family only, small task sets (134 ALFWorld, 100 WebShop). Authors note that reflections can hallucinate and mislead insight extraction.
agent_relevance: Keep both a rule-like summary and a worked example for each stored subgoal; retrieve by task similarity.

source: Song, Pu, Zhao (2026) SkillOps: managing skill libraries
finding: Skill libraries accumulate defects (skill technical debt) that hurt later retrieval and composition. A rule-based maintenance layer improved results.
numbers: ALFWorld: 79.5% standalone, about +8.8 to +8.9 pp over the strongest baseline with no extra task-time LLM calls; as a plug-in it adds +0.68 to +2.90 pp to retrieval-heavy baselines.
limits: Authors' own method on ALFWorld; plug-in gains are small.
agent_relevance: Supports adding library upkeep (retire, merge, re-test items) as a program step, not a model judgement.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) SoK: Agentic skills, beyond tool use in LLM agents
finding: Survey of skills for LLM agents that ties them to Soar's procedural memory and cites SkillsBench. Notes that skills help most in domains thin in pretraining data.
numbers: Cites an earlier SkillsBench version: curated +16.2 pp, self-generated -1.3 pp (the later version reports -8.1 to -11.5 pp for self-generated). Healthcare +51.9 pp, manufacturing +41.9 pp, software engineering +4.5 pp, mathematics +6.0 pp in the cited version.
limits: Secondary source; numbers differ from the later primary paper.
agent_relevance: Use as a map of the literature only; take numbers from the primary papers.

source: Carta et al. (2025) HERAKLES: hierarchical skill compilation for open-ended LLM agents
finding: A reinforcement-learning agent where an LLM picks subgoals and a low-level policy compiles successful behaviour into skills. A learned analogue of chunking, not rule compilation.
numbers: Crafter score, original goals: HERAKLES 39.1, POAD 23.6, FUN 7.8, BOSS 27.6. Synonym goals: HERAKLES 32.8 (-16%), POAD -23%, FUN -26%, BOSS -10% (BOSS drops least in relative terms but from a lower score). Compositional goals at n=4: HERAKLES 19.2 (-51%) versus POAD -92%, FUN -82%, BOSS -64%.
limits: Needs training of a low-level policy, so it is not a prompt-scaffold method. Results section only partly read.
agent_relevance: Compiling subgoals into fast execution holds up better than baselines as goals become more compositional in a trained setting. It does not carry over directly to a frozen-model scaffold.
